title: The June hike rested on cost pass-through already under way
summary: When the ECB raised rates by 25 basis points on 11 June, the Council reached its decision unanimously without debating an alternative proposal. Lagarde described the move as a response to a shock already spreading through the economy. Staff had tested the decision against a milder energy scenario as well as the updated adverse and severe cases. The Council considered the increase warranted even in the milder case. That statement applied to a single decision. It made no commitment to a sequence of increases or a particular terminal rate. The Council had not discussed its position relative to a neutral-rate estimate.

The rise in prices had become broader, though the evidence on wages was materially different from the evidence on other costs. Headline inflation reached 3.2% in May, up from 3.0% in April. Energy inflation was 10.9%, barely higher than the April figure of 10.8%. Food inflation fell to 2.0%, but goods inflation edged up to 0.9% and services accelerated from 3.0% to 3.5%. Together these movements lifted inflation excluding food and energy from 2.2% to 2.5%. Higher non-labour input costs and firms’ selling-price intentions pointed to some indirect effects. Asked specifically about services, Lagarde said it was too early to attribute the whole increase to one mechanism. The wage evidence still showed no clear second-round effects.

The distinction between measured effects and assumptions in a forecast is essential here. Wages and profits had grown more slowly in the first quarter, and wage indicators pointed to further moderation during the year. Nonetheless, the projections built in some second-round effects. Compensation per employee was projected to grow 3.2% in each year from 2026 through 2028. Combined with the projected inflation path, this supported a continued contribution from private consumption. A researcher observing a positive wage assumption should therefore distinguish a forecast of future pay from evidence that bargaining had already reacted to this energy shock.

Headline inflation in the staff baseline averaged 3.0%, 2.3% and 2.0% over the three years, with inflation excluding energy and food at 2.5%, 2.5% and 2.2%. The Council envisaged headline inflation remaining well above target into the first half of 2027 before returning to target in the second half as energy became cheaper and other prices rose more slowly. The projected growth rates were 0.8%, 1.2% and 1.5%. Lagarde saw the increase as a measured response to a sizeable overshoot. The decision did not depend on longer-term expectations having detached from 2%. Short-term measures had risen across market, survey and household indicators, particularly among consumers, while longer-term measures remained broadly anchored.

Some apparently reassuring output evidence also needed interpretation. Adjusting for a temporary Irish factor, first-quarter euro-area output grew with support from domestic demand and exports. Services surveys suggested a slowdown. Manufacturers had held up partly because they were accumulating stocks against disruption and benefiting from defence demand. Inventory accumulation can lift current production while saying little about future final demand. Unemployment was still only 6.3% in April, but labour demand had cooled and job creation slowed. These qualifications explain how the ECB could acknowledge damage to real incomes and near-term investment while still expecting household spending to carry much of the recovery.

Financial conditions had changed little since the previous meeting but remained tighter than before the war. In April the cost of issuing market debt rose to 4.0% while corporate bank loan rates held at 3.6% and mortgage rates at 3.4%. Corporate bank lending grew 3.4% year on year and bond issuance 4.6%. These are observations from before the hike. The financial stability review within the statement judged banks well capitalised and liquid, while identifying abrupt asset-price declines, non-bank amplification and deterioration among energy- or trade-exposed borrowers as risks. An aggregate increase in credit could therefore coexist with growing sensitivity to shocks among particular borrowers.

For investors, the Q&A narrowed the inference to draw from the decision. A benign and short-lived disturbance could ordinarily be looked through, but the Council judged that description no longer fitted. It still saw a difference between a measured increase and the stronger response warranted by a durable, significant deviation. No neutral rate or number of additional meetings was offered as a destination. A defensible study of the communication would therefore examine near-term rates for the decision itself and later forwards for news about persistence, while using sector prices and wages to test the underlying diagnosis.

questions.question: Was the jump in services prices concentrated in activities exposed to fuel?
questions.detail: Compare the prices of transport and other energy-sensitive services with more labour-intensive domestic services. Combine them with selling-price surveys and wage settlements. This would help distinguish indirect input effects that could reverse from a change in labour costs that might sustain inflation after energy prices fell.

questions.question: How much did the new milder scenario change market interpretation?
questions.detail: Compare rates around the initial decision and the Q&A explanation that the hike remained warranted in the milder case. Monitor commodity prices in the same window. A revision to later forwards could indicate news about the Council’s response to alternative outcomes, even if the immediate increase was already priced.

questions.question: Did stockbuilding mask a drop in final demand?
questions.detail: Follow manufacturers’ orders, deliveries and inventories into the next quarter, distinguishing defence demand from private demand where possible. Production sustained to build precautionary stocks can slow sharply when stocks are adequate. That distinction matters for the relative outlook for cyclical borrowers and private fixed investment.

questions.question: How much of the tightening reached bank-dependent firms?
questions.detail: Compare post-hike borrowing rates, standards and loan take-up with bond funding costs for issuers able to use markets. Use April observations as the pre-decision baseline, retaining their publication lag. Different results across the two funding channels would change how the same 25-basis-point move affected spending.
